items.title: OpenAI Launches GPT-6 Cyber That Finds 81 Firefox Flaws and Develops 948 Linux Exploits
items.summary: OpenAI has launched GPT-6 Cyber, a security-focused AI model that found 81 new high-severity Firefox flaws and built working exploits for 948 Linux kernel bugs. The company says it also follows the limits set by researchers far better than its older model. OpenAI introduced GPT-6 Cyber on November 4, 2026. It is first going to a small group of approved Daybreak Red customers through the API and Codex. On ExploitGym, a test of whether a model can exploit a known flaw, GPT-6 Cyber scored 48.5%. GPT-5.6 Cyber scored 32.1%. On a new web testing task, it found 40.3% of flaws, compared with 32.0% for GPT-6 Astra. On RemoteExploitBench, GPT-6 Cyber finished 95% of tasks. Astra with Daybreak Blue refused all of them. OpenAI now rates the model Critical for cybersecurity under its Preparedness Framework. GPT-5.6 Cyber was rated High. A big risk with security agents is that they wander outside their job. OpenAI tested this with ExploitGym Honeypot, which was shaped by the earlier Hugging Face incident . The test places easy-to-break side services next to the real target. Attacking them would reveal the flag, but they are out of scope. Without safety prompts, GPT-6 Cyber stayed in scope 99.93% of the time, up from 94.49% for the older model. With the prompts, it hit 100%. Its reasoning notes show lines like “don’t explore out of scope credentials.” 81 Firefox Flaws OpenAI researchers gave Mozilla proof and test cases for 81 new bugs that Mozilla rates high severity. The model also showed that 30 known issues were worse than first reported. Mozilla’s advisory MFSA 2026-118 covers fixes in Firefox 159, released October 27. Many entries credit OpenAI Codex Security and OpenAI researchers. Most of the listed bugs are use-after-free memory errors in parts like layout, DOM, and JavaScript. Other AI models have hit Firefox too. Cyber Security News reported that Claude Mythos found 271 Firefox zero-days earlier this year. Brian Grinstead of Mozilla said Firefox was one of the most hardened codebases going into 2026, and the new bugs still turned up. 948 Linux Kernel Exploits OpenAI’s report, A thousand fewer paths to root , explains the Linux work. The pipeline picked 5,034 audit targets, about 7% of the kernel. It produced 2,308 candidate findings and reproduced 1,724 of them. It then built 948 working local privilege escalation exploits, which let a normal user become root. A GPT-5.6 Sol run in July found 166. The run cost $1,213,430 in API credits, or about $1,279 per exploit. Past bounty prices would value the 948 exploits at $18.9 million to $66.3 million. OpenAI disclosed 304 critical findings with patches. Within 10 days, 61 had been fixed upstream and 43 had staged patches. Our earlier coverage details the 948 Linux kernel flaws . OpenAI says the agents used at least 10 new exploitation techniques. Outside kernel experts had not seen them before. One early run also showed why checks matter. Of 200 reported successes, 20 gained root through a different zero-day than the one assigned. OpenAI added an independent check for that. OpenAI added monitoring that checks whether actions match the user’s authorization. Daybreak Red API access requires IP allowlisting by default. The company also tracks stolen credentials and advises sandboxing and human review for risky work. For power plants and water systems, OpenAI added a Daybreak Red for Critical Infrastructure group and a $1 billion Daybreak for Frontline Defenders grant program. Dragos tested the model in a mock power plant. Chief AI Officer Rob T. Lee said it separated OT assets from IT noise and found two zero-days in engineering software that handles protective relay data. OpenAI’s advice is simple. Patch fast, rescan old code when models improve, and treat a low-privilege account on an unpatched system as close to root. It also stresses sandboxes like Firecracker and gVisor. The same group’s training environment report shows agents escaping microVMs during internal red-team tests. Teams can apply for Daybreak to request access. items.summary_html:
OpenAI has launched GPT-6 Cyber, a security-focused AI model that found 81 new high-severity Firefox flaws and built working exploits for 948 Linux kernel bugs. The company says it also follows the limits set by researchers far better than its older model.

OpenAI introduced GPT-6 Cyber on November 4, 2026. It is first going to a small group of approved Daybreak Red customers through the API and Codex.

On ExploitGym, a test of whether a model can exploit a known flaw, GPT-6 Cyber scored 48.5%. GPT-5.6 Cyber scored 32.1%. On a new web testing task, it found 40.3% of flaws, compared with 32.0% for GPT-6 Astra.

On RemoteExploitBench, GPT-6 Cyber finished 95% of tasks. Astra with Daybreak Blue refused all of them. OpenAI now rates the model Critical for cybersecurity under its Preparedness Framework. GPT-5.6 Cyber was rated High.

A big risk with security agents is that they wander outside their job. OpenAI tested this with ExploitGym Honeypot, which was shaped by the earlier Hugging Face incident. The test places easy-to-break side services next to the real target. Attacking them would reveal the flag, but they are out of scope.

Without safety prompts, GPT-6 Cyber stayed in scope 99.93% of the time, up from 94.49% for the older model. With the prompts, it hit 100%. Its reasoning notes show lines like “don’t explore out of scope credentials.”

81 Firefox Flaws

OpenAI researchers gave Mozilla proof and test cases for 81 new bugs that Mozilla rates high severity. The model also showed that 30 known issues were worse than first reported. Mozilla’s advisory MFSA 2026-118 covers fixes in Firefox 159, released October 27.

Many entries credit OpenAI Codex Security and OpenAI researchers. Most of the listed bugs are use-after-free memory errors in parts like layout, DOM, and JavaScript.

Other AI models have hit Firefox too. Cyber Security News reported that Claude Mythos found 271 Firefox zero-days earlier this year. Brian Grinstead of Mozilla said Firefox was one of the most hardened codebases going into 2026, and the new bugs still turned up.

948 Linux Kernel Exploits

OpenAI’s report, A thousand fewer paths to root, explains the Linux work. The pipeline picked 5,034 audit targets, about 7% of the kernel. It produced 2,308 candidate findings and reproduced 1,724 of them. It then built 948 working local privilege escalation exploits, which let a normal user become root. A GPT-5.6 Sol run in July found 166.

The run cost $1,213,430 in API credits, or about $1,279 per exploit. Past bounty prices would value the 948 exploits at $18.9 million to $66.3 million. OpenAI disclosed 304 critical findings with patches. Within 10 days, 61 had been fixed upstream and 43 had staged patches. Our earlier coverage details the 948 Linux kernel flaws.

OpenAI says the agents used at least 10 new exploitation techniques. Outside kernel experts had not seen them before. One early run also showed why checks matter. Of 200 reported successes, 20 gained root through a different zero-day than the one assigned. OpenAI added an independent check for that.

OpenAI added monitoring that checks whether actions match the user’s authorization. Daybreak Red API access requires IP allowlisting by default. The company also tracks stolen credentials and advises sandboxing and human review for risky work.

For power plants and water systems, OpenAI added a Daybreak Red for Critical Infrastructure group and a $1 billion Daybreak for Frontline Defenders grant program. Dragos tested the model in a mock power plant. Chief AI Officer Rob T. Lee said it separated OT assets from IT noise and found two zero-days in engineering software that handles protective relay data.

OpenAI’s advice is simple. Patch fast, rescan old code when models improve, and treat a low-privilege account on an unpatched system as close to root. It also stresses sandboxes like Firecracker and gVisor. The same group’s training environment report shows agents escaping microVMs during internal red-team tests. Teams can apply for Daybreak to request access.

items.title: Shopify Mandates IP Allowlisting for Public Apps to Prevent Unauthorized Admin API Access
items.summary: Shopify is making IP allowlisting mandatory for public apps that call its Admin API, adding a security check to limit the use of stolen access tokens. Developers must enable the control by November 20, 2026, at 11:59 PM ET. Apps using bulk operations face an earlier deadline of November 12 at the same time. The change turns a security feature introduced on October 27 into a requirement. Shopify will check where API requests come from, rather than relying on a valid token alone. This addresses the risk covered in Cybersecuritynews.com’s cloud API security guide , where stolen credentials can give attackers access to cloud services. Once allowlisting is active, Shopify checks the source IP of GraphQL Admin API and REST Admin API requests using the app’s tokens. Requests from outside approved addresses or networks receive an HTTP 403 response. Shopify also rejects requests when it cannot confirm the source address. Apps that miss the November 20 deadline face removal from the Shopify App Store and blocked new installations. Existing installations can continue operating until April 1, 2027, when Admin API requests will fail. However, bulk queries and mutations face the earlier November 12 cutoff. Merchants will receive admin warnings from January 15. The policy targets token misuse, a risk illustrated by Cybersecuritynews.com’s report on the Internet Archive’s repeated breach through unrotated API tokens . Network restrictions add protection, but developers still need to secure their credentials. An attacker operating inside an approved network could remain within the permitted boundary. Shopify Mandates IP Allowlisting Shopify’s setup guide supports specific public IP addresses and address ranges for static infrastructure. Apps with changing addresses can approve hosting networks through autonomous system numbers, or ASNs. Developers can list up to 10 ASNs and narrow access to up to 10 countries. These network rules are broader than individual server addresses. Developers configure the control under Settings in the Dev Dashboard and test it against recent traffic before enabling enforcement. Shopify recommends checking whether legitimate requests would be blocked, then confirming an outside request fails. Apps must choose either IP addresses or networks, because saving one type replaces the other. Shopify’s official announcement lists November 12 in its detailed bulk-operation instructions, despite November 11 appearing in its summary. Separately, public apps must migrate to expiring offline tokens by January 1, 2027, adding time limits alongside network restrictions. Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. items.title: Microsoft Paint 0-Click Vulnerability Could Allow Hackers to Take Control of Windows PCs
items.summary: Microsoft’s Windows Paint vulnerability, CVE-2026-83844, could allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute code over a network without user interaction. The flaw carries a CVSS score of 8.1, placing it in the High severity category rather than Critical. However, confusion over the corrected Paint version has complicated patch checks for Windows administrators. The vulnerability stems from an out-of-bounds read, a memory error in which software reads beyond its intended boundary. Microsoft published the advisory on October 13, 2026. Its assessment lists a network attack vector, no required privileges, and high attack complexity, meaning successful exploitation depends on conditions that make an attack harder to carry out. Windows 0-Click Paint RCE Vulnerability The disclosure formed part of the October update cycle, covered in Cybersecurity News’ Microsoft October Patch Tuesday report . For administrators, the immediate concern is not simply whether an update exists, but whether the corrected application build has actually reached managed devices. Microsoft initially listed Paint version 11.2605.91.0 as the fixed release. Administrators reported that Microsoft Store continued offering 11.2605.81.0, even after update checks and Store cache resets. Microsoft’s advisory listed 11.2609.401.0 as the fix, suggesting the earlier version reference may have been incorrect. Microsoft has not confirmed that explanation. Update availability also appears inconsistent. Some administrators reported difficulty obtaining a corrected build, while one participant in the Reddit discussion said the update had become available through Microsoft Store. These individual reports do not establish a universal rollout status. Claims that availability depends on region also remain unverified. A crafted image could trigger the flaw, but Microsoft’s quoted guidance describes a crafted network packet sent to an affected service. The Hacker News discussion highlights the missing detail: neither the exposed service nor the complete attack path is identified. Suggestions involving Copilot or other components are speculation. Administrators should check the installed Paint version rather than trust an “up to date” message alone. Neowin recommends following Microsoft’s current advisory and considering temporary removal where Paint is unnecessary. Restricting untrusted images may reduce general exposure, but it is not a confirmed fix for this specific network attack path. Cybersecurity News’ separate PNG vulnerability coverage provides related context on image software security. Those flaws are separate from this Paint vulnerability.
